entries.title: Trump heads to South Carolina to boost Senator Darline Graham in race
entries.summary: The race between the sister of late Senator Lindsey Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews has tightened in deep-red state.
entries.content:
Race between sibling of former Senator Lindsey Graham, Democrat Annie Andrews has tightened in deep-red state.

United States President Donald Trump is set to travel to South Carolina to boost the campaign of Darline Graham, the sister of his close ally, the late Senator Lindsey Graham.

The visit on Wednesday, which will include a rally alongside Graham, comes as the Senate race in deep-red South Carolina has grown uncomfortably close for Republicans.

Lindsey Graham, long one of the most hawkish members of the Senate who was an outspoken supporter of the US-Israel war on Iran, had been expected to sail to victory in the November 3 vote. But his unexpected death in July upended the race.

South Carolina’s governor tapped Darline Graham to finish her brother’s term. Trump then made the surprise move of endorsing Graham in a new Republican primary, helping her to claim the party’s nomination. The president said the endorsement was “in honour of her brother”.

In a video message last week, Trump again said Graham had his unconditional support.

“I’m asking everyone in South Carolina to get out and vote for a wonderful person, a great woman … a woman that Lindsey Graham said is the greatest person he’s ever met,” Trump said.

Democratic challenger Annie Andrews, a medical doctor and paediatrician, has seized on Graham’s inexperience and her unorthodox route to the Republican nomination.

Speaking to a local Fox News affiliate before Trump’s rally in Pendleton, South Carolina, Andrews pointed to Graham’s lacklustre debate performance, including one instance where she said she was “not that informed on national security”.

“My opponent needs the highest level of federal government politicians to speak for her. On the debate stage, it was really clear,” Andrews said.

Graham, meanwhile, has called Andrews “the most radical liberal that’s ever run for state office in South Carolina”.

Polls have shown Graham leading by about 2.7 percentage points, according to a Real Clear Politics average. Trump carried the state by 18 percentage points in 2024.

Tensions on Russia

Trump’s visit comes after the president issued an executive order waiving most sanctions and tariffs on Russia, established by a law named after Lindsey Graham and passed with bipartisan support in 2026.

The move prompted a tempered rebuke from Darline Graham.

“Personally, I would choose to put the ⁠pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down,” she told The Associated Press news agency on Saturday.

“I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia,” she said.

The executive order on sanctions has been part of a wider Trump administration shift in its approach to ending the war with Ukraine, which began with Russia’s invasion in February 2024.

Trump and his allies have heaped pressure on Ukraine, framing its leader, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as the main impediment to peace. In turn, Washington has offered several concessions to Russia, including a deal to buy Russian diesel.

Lindsey Graham had been a staunch supporter of Ukraine. His death came shortly after he returned from his 10th visit to the country since the war began.

Political headwinds

The tightening race in South Carolina underscores the harsh political reality for Republicans heading into the final stretch of the midterms.

Trump has sought to use his political clout to bring party loyalists out to vote, campaigning in strongholds across the country. But the president heads into the vote with the lowest approval ratings of his career, with voters expressing dismay about affordability and the knock-on effects of the US-Israel war with Iran.

Beyond South Carolina, other one-time Republican strongholds have shown signs of shifting towards Democrats.

That includes Kansas, where polls suggest Republican Ashley Hinson is effectively tied with Democrat Joshua Turek. The state, where farmers have been particularly hard hit by rising prices on fuel and equipment, has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1939.

Trump also broke from the Republican establishment to endorse Attorney General Ken Paxton over Senator John Cornyn in the Texas primary. Polling averages show Paxton, whose career has been marred by a procession of scandals, trailing behind Democratic challenger Talarico by 1.7 percentage points. The race is widely considered a toss-up.

A Republican has not won statewide office in Texas since 1994.

entries.title: Judge orders Meta to pay $25bn in fines for Facebook privacy violations
entries.summary: A jury found Meta guilty of lying to Facebook users in ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠New Mexico about access to their data.
entries.content:
A jury found Meta guilty of lying to Facebook users in ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠New Mexico about access to their data.

A United States judge has ordered Meta to pay $25bn after a jury found the company misled Facebook users about privacy violations, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.

New Mexico state District Judge Francis Mathew issued the ruling on Wednesday.

“Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false,” he said.

Last month, a jury found Meta responsible for more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws. New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez highlighted that the decision was one of the largest state verdicts against a company in US history.

“This judgement should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” Torrez said at a news conference.

Meta lawyer Matt Nicholson argued in court that a sum as high as $40bn would be “shocking to the conscience”, while a lawyer for New Mexico, Randi McGinn, urged standing up to “tech titans who think they are bulletproof and can do whatever they want”.

“The jury didn’t make findings that any New Mexican heard or saw these statements, or was harmed by them,” Nicholson argued during a hearing held early this month.

Torrez told reporters following the verdict that all the money awarded would go into a fund for the state’s education system.

The amount awarded in the case far exceeds the $5bn fine that the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019.

New Mexico accused Meta of misleading users about who could access their personal information and how harmful content was handled on its platforms. Jurors found that 26 of 29 statements made by Meta and its leadership on privacy and content moderation were misleading.

Meta plans to appeal the verdict, potentially reducing the final payment amount.

In a statement, CJ Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.

“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Mahoney said. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”

The lawsuit, filed in 2021, stemmed partly from revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm that is now defunct, had obtained personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users without their consent and used it to develop targeted political advertisements. Its clients included President Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign.

The case, a major setback for the tech giant, marks the second legal defeat for Meta in New Mexico in six months. In March, a jury found the company misled users about the safety of young people on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, ordering it to pay $375m in civil penalties. Meta was later ordered to make an additional $567m payment into a state fund for teen mental health and was required to implement measures to protect young users.

entries.title: Will Russia’s diesel shipment to the US lower prices before midterms?
entries.summary: Moscow dispatches its inaugural diesel shipment to the US, aiming to ease fuel shortages as midterm elections loom.
entries.content:
Moscow dispatches its inaugural diesel shipment to the US, aiming to ease fuel shortages as midterm elections loom.

Russia is set to send its first tanker carrying diesel fuel to the United States on Thursday, as part of an agreement with Washington aimed at easing fuel shortages that have pushed US diesel prices higher before next month’s midterm elections.

Moscow announced on Wednesday that the tanker was headed to an undisclosed US port and was scheduled to depart on Thursday. The shipment is part of a broader effort to send more fuel to the US, even as Russia faces its own supply constraints and US consumers grapple with elevated prices at the pump.

The announcement comes as the White House seeks to contain rising energy costs as cost-of-living concerns weigh on Americans in the run-up to the contentious midterm elections.

Voters increasingly trust Democrats over Republicans on economic issues, according to a recent Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, with 37 percent of voters believing Democrats are more trusted on economics and 28 percent trusting Republicans more, while confidence in President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy has slumped, with 28 percent approving of Trump’s handling of the economy.

The first shipment was announced during a visit to St Petersburg by US special envoy Steve Witkoff, who held talks with Russian officials.

Is this a single shipment or multiple?

The first tanker is part of a broader commitment to increase Russian fuel supplies to the US, rather than a one-off delivery.

Trump had previously said Russia would export 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel. It would be followed by another 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”.

Russian officials said on Wednesday that the initial shipment would be the first of several.

However, the scale and timing of those shipments remain uncertain. Russia has been dealing with domestic fuel shortages linked to Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries, which have disrupted refining capacity and forced Moscow to introduce restrictions on fuel exports.

The ability to fulfil the promised deliveries will depend on how quickly Russia can restore production while meeting its own domestic demand.

The deal also comes after Trump called off plans for another round of sanctions targeting Russia. Among the proposed measures was a 100 percent tariff on goods from major purchasers of Russian crude oil, including China and India.

Will the shipment lower prices before the midterms?

Analysts say the first shipment is unlikely to deliver meaningful relief to US consumers before the midterm elections. US retail diesel prices topped $6 a gallon ($1.59 per litre) in September and have remained elevated.

On Wednesday, the national average stood at $6.31 a gallon ($1.67 per litre), according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), down from $6.51 ($1.72 per litre) a month earlier, marking a 3.1 percent decrease but still significantly higher than this time last year, at $3.62 ($0.96 per litre).

“The volumes Russia can provide are small in comparison to the global shortage and US’s own production. The cargo is unlikely to have a meaningful impact on supply or meaningfully lower the price,” Rachel Ziemba, an adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.

“The reported shipment is equivalent to roughly two hours of US distillate consumption. Even if it arrives as planned, it will make very little difference to national supply,” Aarathi Krishnan, CEO of Raksha Intelligence, told Al Jazeera.

The first tanker may not even reach the US before voters head to the polls, Ziemba said. Departing on Thursday would mark the beginning of its journey, not the date the fuel becomes available to consumers.

Any sustained reduction in prices would depend on a broader improvement in global supply, rather than a single delivery.

“Russia’s ability to supply more diesel depends partly on the condition of its refineries. Ukraine’s attacks affect those facilities. And Washington’s desire for lower fuel prices creates an interest in reducing that disruption,” Krishnan added.

Would a ceasefire impact fuel prices long term?

A long-term ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine could help ease pressure on energy markets by allowing damaged Russian refineries to be rebuilt and production to increase.

“This [the current agreement] is more about political posturing to get the US to further increase pressure on Ukraine and align with Russia,” Ziemba said.

She added that meaningful relief for the global oil market would depend in large part on developments in the Middle East, particularly the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping route through which roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas supplies passed before the US-Israel attack on Iran.

The Russian shipment comes as conflict involving Iran and disruptions to energy shipping have intensified pressure on global fuel markets more broadly. There were at least 18 attacks on vessels over the previous two weeks, according to Kpler, a data analytics platform. On Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told the Financial Times that Iran was fully prepared to defend itself.

The Russian agreement is unlikely to resolve the underlying supply problem on its own without a chance to rebuild its refineries.

“The agreement may help individual buyers or provide some immediate reassurance to traders. But sustained price relief will depend on actual increases in available diesel, which Russia has not yet demonstrated it can deliver,” Krishnan said.

entries.title: Cuba accuses US of threatening countries ahead of UN embargo vote
entries.summary: Havana says Washington is threatening countries with retaliation if they refuse to vote against condemning its embargo.
entries.content:
Havana says Washington is threatening countries with retaliation if they refuse to vote against condemning its embargo.

Cuba has accused the United States of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions and other retaliatory measures in an effort to get them to change their votes on an upcoming United Nations resolution calling for an end to the long-running embargo against the island.

Every year, a majority in the UN General Assembly votes in favour of a nonbinding resolution seeking a stop to the US embargo, which began in the early 1960s.

The embargo, considered the longest in modern history, has been credited with exacerbating economic hardship on the island.

But on Wednesday, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said that the administration of US President Donald Trump was seeking to pressure members of the UN General Assembly to vote against the resolution this year.

He explained that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Washington’s ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz were personally leading the campaign, which he alleged had been going on for months.

“It is a new and dangerous way of conducting multilateral diplomacy,” Rodriguez wrote in a statement on the social media platform X. “It reflects the impotence of those who know they are in the wrong and whose only remaining recourse is force.”

Rodriguez said US officials had threatened to suspend cooperation programmes, deny visas to government officials and their families, and even back opposition parties in upcoming elections if countries refused to change their positions.

He also accused the US of urging some countries to abstain or skip the vote altogether if they were unwilling to vote against Cuba.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the US State Department and the US Mission to the UN for comment, but it did not receive a reply by the time of publication.

Heightening pressure on Cuba

The allegations come amid escalating tensions between the two countries ahead of the vote on the resolution, expected to take place on October 27 or 28.

The Trump administration has long maintained that the Cuban government — not the embargo — is to blame for the country’s struggling economy, and it has called for regime change.

On Monday, Waltz accused Cuban diplomats of harassing and intimidating participants at a US-hosted panel on alleged human rights abuses in Cuba.

Cuba’s UN Ambassador Ernesto Soberon Guzman and other representatives had confronted Waltz as he left the event at UN headquarters in New York City.

Speaking to reporters afterward, Waltz said that, every year, the Cuban government “propagates a lie through its annual resolution”.

“It uses excuse after excuse to justify its oppression, to justify the misery of the Cuban people, and what we are doing here at the US Mission to the UN is exposing those lies,” he said.

In a separate briefing that day, Waltz also acknowledged that Washington had been lobbying European countries to reconsider their support for the resolution. He pointed to allegations from Ukraine that Cuban nationals fighting for Russia weren’t being paid and that the money was instead going to the Cuban government.

“Yes, we’ve asked many of our European colleagues: Given this evidence from the Ukrainian government, how can they continue to vote for this resolution that is a propaganda tool for the Cuban regime and that is directly affecting their national security?” Waltz said.

The UN General Assembly has voted overwhelmingly in support of resolutions calling for an end to the US economic embargo on Cuba almost every year since 1992. The embargo itself has been in place for more than six decades.

Since the start of 2026, the Trump administration has intensified pressure on Cuba by blocking oil supplies and threatening tariffs on countries supplying the country with fuel, leaving Cubans to face more severe shortages of essential supplies and prolonged blackouts.

entries.title: UK Conservative Party suspends ex-candidate after Al Jazeera investigation
entries.summary: The UK's Conservatives suspend former candidate Jack Ross after he was filmed discussing hiring contract killers.
entries.content:
The UK’s Conservatives suspend former candidate Jack Ross after he was filmed discussing hiring contract killers.

The UK’s Conservative Party has suspended Jack Ross, a former election candidate and party member, after an Al Jazeera documentary showed him discussing the cost of hiring contract killers and offering to broker the services of a far-right activist with alleged paramilitary links.

Al Jazeera’s undercover investigation, Contract Killers and the Far Right, began in 2021 when an undercover reporter joined Turning Point UK (TPUK), an independent offshoot of the right-wing US activist group Turning Point USA.

TPUK has close ties to several senior British Conservative Party members, as well as to leaders of Reform UK.

TPUK’s CEO Jack Ross stood as a Conservative Party candidate in 2023. Ross introduced Al Jazeera’s undercover reporter to Nesbitt, who is from Glasgow, Scotland.

“Mr Ross’s membership of the Conservative party has been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation. We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing,” a Conservative Party spokesperson told The Guardian.

Ross also told Al Jazeera’s undercover operative that for “a certain amount”, Nesbitt and his contacts could arrange physical attacks.

“They can kick the f*** out of someone. They can start cutting people’s faces up. That’s another amount. They can stab someone,” Ross said. “They can shoot someone. They could kill someone.”
